text: Every major cloud provider now encrypts your data at rest by default, which is a relatively recent and genuinely good shift. This lesson looks at what 'at rest' actually means, which real services do it automatically, and exactly what threat that protection does and doesn't cover.

Azure Storage Accounts, Azure Managed Disks, Amazon S3, and Amazon EBS volumes are all encrypted at rest using AES-256 by default now — you don't flip a switch or write a line of code to turn it on. The provider generates an encryption key, encrypts your data with it before writing to physical storage, and decrypts it automatically when an authorized request reads it back. This used to be an optional, extra-cost feature on both platforms; today it's simply the default state for nearly every storage service you'll touch.

'At rest' specifically means data sitting on a physical disk, SSD, or tape, rather than data moving across a network or actively being processed in memory. The real threat it defends against is physical access to the underlying hardware — a decommissioned drive pulled from a data center, a stolen backup tape, or a technician handling a failed disk. Without encryption at rest, that physical media would hold your raw, readable data; with it, the media holds unreadable ciphertext, useless without the key.

Encryption at rest does not protect you from someone who already has valid, authorized access to your data through the normal API or portal — a leaked access key, an over-permissioned IAM role, or a compromised admin account can all still read your data in plain form, because the cloud platform decrypts it transparently for any authorized request. At rest encryption is a defense against stolen hardware, not a substitute for access control, identity, or network security covered in Chapters 1 and 2.

Cloud providers handle the encryption itself automatically, but somebody still controls the key doing that encrypting. Next up: Azure Key Vault and AWS KMS, the two services that actually generate, store, and manage those keys.
